store.0: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year, and my schedule this semester is quite packed. I'm finally taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to be at this stage, as it feels like just yesterday I was learning about simple data structures in an intro class. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's exciting to see how far I've come!
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by theory that directly connects to real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. We've been exploring dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It's mind-bending, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing.
store.2: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, my second-hardest class this semester is Distributed Systems(CS 2631). It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project simulating a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure, as we have to collaborate with folks who have different coding styles and ideas about the final product. However, that's also its beauty. In real-world settings, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures. It's nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in a config file. But once we fixed it and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. The professor is from the industry and worked on a couple of indie games that got some traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even user experience design. It's incredibly fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was challenging, but it was rewarding to see it come together.
store.4: I initially thought I'd regret signing up for Introduction to Quantum Computing, but now I actually enjoy it. The professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math, which makes it more accessible. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not building actual quantum computers, but we're modeling algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff that has made me rethink how I approach problems.
store.5: My Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to stay organized. One person on our team is the designated Scrum Master, so we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it applies to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding in my other classes. It's nice to sit back and analyze abstract ideas. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.7: My typical college schedule is a juggling act. Mondays and Wednesdays are packed. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it adds to the workload.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. Capstone alone can consume around ten hours a week, and that's without considering bugs or model training issues. The Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group meets at least twice a week, and we rely on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a nightmare, but it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of a job environment. It's a unique opportunity to explore and experiment without any real-world constraints.
store.9: I'm having a blast this semester. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's not as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, collaborate, and think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a great feeling.
